Remote sensing is the acquisition of information about an object or area from a distance, without touching it, as opposed to measuring it on-site observation. The term often refers to observing Earth from satellites or aircraft, but also covers studies of other planets and some ship- or ground-based methods, such as sonar.
Remote sensing produces the satellite views in online maps and the cloud imagery shown in weather forecasts.

In current usage, the term remote sensing generally refers to the use of satellite- or airborne-based sensor technologies to detect and classify objects on Earth.

It may be split into "active" remote sensing (when a signal is emitted by a sensor mounted on a satellite or aircraft to the object and its reflection is detected by the sensor) and "passive" remote sensing (when the reflection of sunlight is detected by the sensor).
Overview

Remote sensing methods are generally classed as passive or active. Passive sensors record natural energy that an object or scene emits or reflects, sunlight reflected by the surface is the source they most often measure. Common passive instruments include photography, both film and digital, as well as radiometers and spectrometers.

These often operate in the visible, infrared, thermal infrared and microwave bands. Active sensors supply their own energy: they direct radiation at a target, and then detect and measure what is reflected or scattered back from the target.

Radar and lidar are active systems that time the interval between sending a pulse and receiving its return, which can give the distance to the target. Repeated or Doppler measurements can establish a target's speed and direction.

Remote sensing allows data to be gathered from areas that are dangerous or difficult to reach. In polar regions for example, large distances and low temperatures hamper ground studies of glaciers, ice shelves and ice sheets, so researchers rely on airborne and satellite measurements.
Brazil's National Institute for Space Research has measured deforestation in the Amazon Basin every year since 1988 using Landsat-class imagery.

Shallow coastal waters can be surveyed with airborne bathymetric lidar, which is safer and more efficient then sending survey crews out by boat, and remote sensing has been used to map the topography of the ocean floor.

During the Cold War, most American aerial reconnaissance was flown along the borders and casts of the Soviet Union at a distance, rather than over its territory. More generally, remote sensing can replace slower and most expensive fieldwork without disturbing the area or object being studied.

Combined with aircraft, ship and ground-based measurement, these data enable researchers to study natural phenomena over short and long timescales. El Niño for example is tracked by merging satellite altimetry with readings from moored buoys in the tropical Pacific.
Other uses include natural resource management, mapping wildlife habitat for conservation, greenhouse gas monitoring, oil spill detection and monitoring, and national security.
Data acquisition

The basis for multispectral collection and analysis is that of examined areas or objects that reflect or emit radiation that stand out from surrounding areas. For a summary of major remote sensing satellite systems see the overview table.
Radar

Conventional radar is mostly associated with air traffic control, early warning, and certain large-scale meteorological data. Doppler radar is used by local law enforcements' monitoring of speed limits and in enhanced meteorological collection such as wind speed and direction within weather systems in addition to precipitation location and intensity.

Other types of active collection includes plasmas in the ionosphere. Interferometric synthetic aperture radar is used to produce precise digital elevation models of large scale terrain (See RADARSAT, TerraSAR-X, Magellan). Laser and radar altimeters on satellites have provided a wide range of data.

By measuring the bulges of water caused by gravity, they map features on the seafloor to a resolution of a mile or so. By measuring the height and wavelength of ocean waves, the altimeters measure wind speeds and direction, and surface ocean currents and directions.
Ultrasound (acoustic) and radar tide gauges are used to measure sea level, tides and wave direction in coastal and offshore tide gauges.
Light detection and ranging (LiDAR)

Light detection and ranging (LiDAR) is used for weapon ranging, laser illuminated homing of projectiles, and to detect and measure the concentration of various chemicals in the atmosphere while airborne LiDAR can be used to measure the heights of objects and features on the ground more accurately than radar technology.

LiDAR can be used to detect ground surface changes typically by creating Digital Surface Models (DSMs) or Digital Elevation Models (DEMs). Vegetation remote sensing is a principal application of LIDAR.
Radiometers and Photometers

The most common instruments in use are radiometers and photometers, which collect reflected and emitted radiation in a wide range of frequencies. The most prevalent of these frequencies are visible and infrared sensors, followed by microwave, gamma-ray, and rarely, ultraviolet.

They may also be used to detect the emission spectra of various chemicals, providing data on chemical concentrations in the atmosphere. Radiometers are also used at night, as artificial light emissions are a key signature of human activity. Applications include remote sensing of population, GDP, and damage to infrastructure from war or disasters.
Radiometers and radar onboard of satellites can be also used to monitor volcanic eruptions.

Aerial platforms and Satellites

Stereoscopic pairs of aerial photographs have often been used to make topographic maps by imagery and terrain analysts in trafficability and highway departments for potential routes, in addition to modelling terrestrial habitat features.

Simultaneous multi-spectral platforms such as Landsat have been in use since the early 1970s. These thematic mappers take images in multiple wavelengths and are usually found on Earth observation satellites, including (for example) the Landsat program or the IKONOS satellite.

Maps of land cover and land use from thematic mapping can be used to prospect for minerals, detect or monitor land usage, detect invasive vegetation, deforestation, and examine the health of indigenous plants and crops (satellite crop monitoring), including entire farming regions or forests.

Prominent scientists using remote sensing for this purpose include Janet Franklin and Ruth DeFries. Landsat images are used by regulatory agencies such as KYDOW to indicate water quality parameters including Secchi depth, chlorophyll density, and total phosphorus content. Weather satellites are used in meteorology and climatology.
False Color Composites (FCCs) and Pseudocolor

A major remote sensing application, used broadly across fields such as urban planning and environmental studies, is False Color Composites (FCCs) and Pseudocolor maps. An FCC is a color-rendering method in which a true-color image (a photograph or image that the human eye would render) is altered to appear in different colors.

The purpose is typically to identify patterns the human eye cannot normally detect, or highlight certain land cover uses. Pseudocolor uses one spectral band and maps it to a new color spectrum rather than the original gray band.
FCCs and Pseudocolor mapping remain vital tools for visualizing data spatially by allowing researchers to treat non-visible wavelengths as visible.
== False Color Composite ==
Humans use three spectral bands to perceive color: red, green, and blue. Remote sensing platforms such as ArcGIS and QGIS similarly compose images using three color bands.

Therefore, a true color image assigns red light wavelengths (620-750 nm) to the red band, and green and blue light wavelengths (495-570 nm and 450-485 nm) to the green and blue bands, respectively. FCCs are easily made by rearranging which wavelengths on the electromagnetic spectrum are assigned to certain color bands.
